title: Judges 11:1–11
context: Israel has again turned to other gods and been oppressed, this time by Ammon east of the Jordan (10:6–18). The elders of Gilead need a commander. They turn to Jephthah, a capable warrior whom his half-brothers had driven out because his mother was a prostitute, and who had been living in Tob with a band of outlaws. Jephthah bargains for leadership: if the LORD gives victory, he will be head over Gilead. The agreement is sealed before the LORD at Mizpah. Many readers notice a parallel with the preceding chapter, where Israel rejected the LORD and then came back to him in distress. Both traditions see God raising a deliverer from the margins and working through flawed people, without approving everything they do.

verses.text: Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty man of valor. He was the son of a prostitute. Gilead became the father of Jephthah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah is introduced as a mighty man of valor, the son of Gilead by a prostitute. His origins mark him as an outsider.

Arminian readers note that God’s calling is open to those whom society rejects. Jephthah’s background does not disqualify him from being used by God, and he is responsible for how he answers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God sovereignly chooses unlikely instruments, as with Rahab (Joshua 2), so that the glory belongs to him rather than to human status.

Both traditions see God working through people with painful histories, which offers hope to all who feel excluded.

verses.text: Gilead’s wife bore him sons. When his wife’s sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, “You will not inherit in our father’s house, for you are the son of another woman.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Gilead’s other sons drive Jephthah out, refusing him an inheritance because he is the son of another woman. Family rejection shapes his life.

Arminian readers note that the brothers’ choice is a real wrong done to Jephthah, for which they are responsible before God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Scripture does not hide the sins of families, and that God can bring good from injustice (compare Genesis 50:20).

Both traditions read the verse with compassion for Jephthah and see in it a warning against excluding others because of their origins.

verses.text: Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Outlaws joined up with Jephthah, and they went out with him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah flees to Tob, and outlaws gather around him. He becomes the leader of a band on the margins.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah’s circumstances shaped him, yet he still made choices about how to live. Exclusion does not remove responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the parallel with David, around whom the distressed and discontented gathered (1 Samuel 22:2). God prepares leaders in unlikely places.

Both traditions avoid idealizing Jephthah’s band while recognizing that God can redeem a life lived on the edges.

verses.text: After a while, the children of Ammon made war against Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Some time later, Ammon makes war against Israel. The crisis creates the need for a deliverer.

Arminian readers note that the oppression follows Israel’s unfaithfulness described in chapter 10, and that God’s discipline aims to bring repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God uses even the hostility of nations to accomplish his purposes in disciplining and delivering his people.

Both traditions read the war within the cycle of Judges: sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance, showing both God’s justice and his mercy.

verses.text: When the children of Ammon made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to get Jephthah out of the land of Tob.
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders of Gilead go to Tob to bring Jephthah back. Those who rejected him now need him.

Arminian readers note the irony: the community that excluded Jephthah must now humble itself and seek his help, a choice it makes under pressure.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s providence turns rejection into calling. The one cast out becomes the one sought out.

Both traditions see a pattern that Christians often connect with Christ, the stone the builders rejected (Psalm 118:22), while holding the comparison loosely.

verses.text: They said to Jephthah, “Come and be our chief, that we may fight with the children of Ammon.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders ask Jephthah to be their chief so that they can fight Ammon. Their offer is practical, not repentant.

Arminian readers note that the elders seek Jephthah for what he can do for them, without first acknowledging the wrong done to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the people’s motives are mixed, yet God works through them to bring deliverance. His purposes are not limited by human imperfection.

Both traditions see in this exchange a mirror of how people often approach God himself, seeking help in crisis without full repentance.

verses.text: Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “Didn’t you hate me, and drive me out of my father’s house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah reminds them that they hated him and drove him out, and asks why they come now in distress. His question exposes their past.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah’s words echo God’s rebuke to Israel in 10:13–14, where Israel came to God only in trouble.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the parallel highlights how Israel treats both God and his servants: rejecting them and then returning in need.

Both traditions draw from the verse a call to honest repentance rather than mere crisis-driven appeals.

verses.text: The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “Therefore we have turned again to you now, that you may go with us and fight with the children of Ammon. You will be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders say they have turned back to him so that he can lead them against Ammon and be head over Gilead. They raise their offer.

Arminian readers note that the elders make a real commitment, and their word will be binding before God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the language of turning back echoes repentance, though here it is pragmatic. God uses even partial turning to accomplish his purposes.

Both traditions observe that the negotiation reveals human calculation, while God remains the true deliverer behind the scenes.

verses.text: Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “If you bring me home again to fight with the children of Ammon, and the LORD delivers them before me, will I be your head?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah asks whether, if the LORD gives him victory, he will be their head. He names the LORD as the source of victory.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah acknowledges God’s role, even while bargaining for his own position. Faith and self-interest are mixed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Jephthah’s words show some knowledge of the LORD as the giver of victory, though his bargaining foreshadows the later vow.

Both traditions see in Jephthah a man of real but imperfect faith, a pattern Hebrews 11:32 later acknowledges.

verses.text: The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “The LORD will be witness between us. Surely we will do what you say.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The elders swear that the LORD will be witness between them. The agreement is made before God.

Arminian readers note that the oath binds both parties to faithfulness, and that God holds people accountable for their promises.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that calling on the LORD as witness reflects Israel’s understanding that God sees and judges all agreements.

Both traditions affirm the seriousness of oaths made in God’s name, a theme that becomes painfully important in Jephthah’s vow later in the chapter.

verses.text: Then Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and chief over them. Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD in Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jephthah goes with the elders, the people make him head and chief, and he speaks all his words before the LORD at Mizpah. The agreement is confirmed in worship.

Arminian readers note that Jephthah brings his commitment before God, seeking his presence in a solemn moment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the public confirmation before the LORD gives the agreement religious weight. Leadership in Israel is meant to rest under God’s authority.

Both traditions see value in bringing major decisions before God, while noting that Jephthah’s later words show the danger of speaking rashly in God’s name.
